Five Methods of Apportionment

Game: The original calculator was created for Peter Tannenbaum's Excursions in Modern Mathematics and reproduced with permission; this is an independent implementation of the same five methods.
How to play: Change the seat count, state count or a population, then compare the five allocations side by side.
Seats 23 States 3
Look for the math

Five ways to share seats in proportion to population, and five different answers. Each method chooses a rounding rule, then either adjusts the divisor or hands out the leftovers.

Two families of methods

Hamilton rounds every standard quota down and gives the leftover seats to the largest fractional parts. The other four are divisor methods: Jefferson rounds down, Adams rounds up, Webster rounds to the nearest whole number, and Huntington-Hill rounds up only past the geometric mean of n and n+1. They can be computed by giving each seat in turn to the state with the largest priority under the method's rule.

Why the choices differ

Small changes in population can move seats between states in surprising ways. Hamilton suffers the famous paradoxes: adding seats to the house can cost a state a seat, and a faster-growing state can lose one to a slower-growing rival. The divisor methods avoid those paradoxes but can violate the quota rule — giving a state a seat outside its exact quota. There is no method that avoids every problem.

What the check found

The logic test checks two thousand random countries. All five methods always allocate exactly the number of seats, the four divisor methods follow their own priority rules, and Hamilton and Adams agree with the separate dedicated ports on this site. It also pins down a concrete Alabama paradox. Try a state with zero population: no method should give it a seat.

Set three states and twenty-three seats. Which methods agree, and which single state do they disagree about?
